title: Resident Evil: Apocalypse
full_review:
In "Resident Evil: Apocalypse" (Screen Gems) -- the apocalyptically preposterous and unremittingly violent sequel to 2002's equally mindless "Resident Evil" -- a handful of humans must once again fight for survival against legions of flesh-eating zombies. Only this time, the ghouls are hungrier and the guy in charge of the fake blood racks up overtime pay.

Both action horror movies are based on the ultraviolent video game of the same name, which means expect more ammo rounds than two-syllable words.

The new film opens with a quick recap, a somewhat superfluous gesture since the plots of both films combined amount to little more than: See zombies, shoot zombies. Milla Jovovich returns as Alice, former head of security for the shadowy Umbrella Corporation, the company responsible for developing the deadly virus that causes the undead epidemic.

In the original, the outbreak was confined to Umbrella's secret underground facility known as the "Hive," but in "Apocalypse" the pathogen has spread to the surface population, turning those infected into slow-footed freaks with a serious case of the munchies.

In an effort to quarantine the contagion, Umbrella's sinister honcho, Major Cain (Thomas Kretschmann), orders all exit roads sealed. Alice, one of only two survivors from the first film, has since been biogenetically altered by Umbrella, resulting in her having enhanced strength, speed and agility, all of which come into play during her frenetic zombie-whupping fight sequences.
With shades of John Carpenter's "Escape from New York," Alice leads a ragtag band of survivors as they try to rescue the young daughter of Umbrella's disenfranchised top scientist (Jared Harris), who has secretly guaranteed them safe passage out of the hot zone if they accomplish their mission.

As if being chased by the city's decaying denizens wasn't trouble enough, Cain also unleashes an indestructible -- and cheesy-looking -- mutant named Nemesis to track the group down and destroy them. He also plans to drop a nuclear bomb on the city at sunrise to cover up Umbrella's little secret. Nothing quite says discreet like a mushroom cloud.

Other potential zombie meals include Jill Valentine (Sienna Guillory), a female cop clad in a miniskirt and stilettos -- what else would you wear to fight zombies? -- and Carlos Olivera (Oded Fehr), a member of Umbrella's elite security squad.

As directed by Alexander Witt, this "Dawn of the Dead" clone is devoid of anything remotely resembling narrative, character development or redeeming moral value. Instead, Witt opts for nonstop, lavishly violent action sequences -- including one in a church -- which ultimately go nowhere, and are as tedious as they are gratuitous. But what do you expect from a filmmaker who cut his teeth shooting car chases as second unit director on movies like "Speed" and "The Italian Job"? Perhaps just as telling is the flick's end crawl which contains credits for "undead stripper #2" and "featured 'surplus' undead #3."

Unfortunately, given the video game's popularity, "Resident Evil: Apocalypse" is practically guaranteed a big opening weekend. The film's open-door ending suggests that there are more zombies on the way, which would point to an audience eager to watch stylized violence packaged as entertainment. Now that's scary!

Due to excessive violence and gore, desecration of religious objects and brief partial nudity, as well as recurring rough language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
